That wasn't a custom before the schism — I suppose it's an easy way to distinguish our wargs from their wargs." You've seen the silvered barding that her warg wears, as with some of the other beasts prowling the palace with their guard handlers. It's very pretty, but also looks to be more ceremonial than anything else. "It vexes Norathar to no end — very constraining, and she can't wait for the end of the day for us to return so she can take it off. But we all make sacrifices for peace, and even she has to admit that discomfort is a small price to pay for our success. When in the palace, do as the snobs do, I suppose. They didn't even have one tailored for her — it was a hand-me-down from another bitch to be provided on short notice, and she complains about the lingering scent all day." Hah... "If that's the greatest of my complaints — or at least, those that don't come as part and parcel of my task — I guess I've got it pretty good. Plus, Norathar acknowledges that her discomfort isn't much compared to what I have to do day in, day out — she's such a sanguine pup." |"Yesterday, I took several of the other druids out to the city at large — under guard, of course — to see what had become of the Winter City in their absence. Most of them agree that they don't want to live in the city walls proper even after re-integration; there's talk of outlying settlements within reach of the city proper. Close enough to be available, far enough to not place undue strain on the Winter City's infrastructure." That doesn't bode very well for re-integration of them, though, not to mention the reunification of the pale elves as a people. Still, it's a step forward. "Even before the schism, we were a bit removed from boer'alvar society — the temples to the Old Wyld were where druids would mingle with the people at large. Now that they've been repurposed as temples to this Lumia goddess — " her face crumples up into a scowl — "there's even less reason for us to have an established presence in the Winter City. The people seem happy worshipping Lumia... happier than they were under the old scheme of things." That's... that's very honest of her to be able to admit as much. That realization must have been a bitter pill to swallow. "It was, but it's the truth. The wyld trees were right — we can't really compete with the likes of that. There's no way we can provoke some kind of revival in the people of the Winter City — they can't go back, not after we failed them so deeply. The others will call this defeatist talk, but we have to move on. It was a while before I realized this for myself, walking down the streets of the Winter City... hopefully they'll come around to it on their own as well." |"To be honest, I don't know how to feel about staying here. Legend has it that the Old Wyld aided in the making of the palace, carving the palace both out of and into the glacier; when that was done, boer'alvar hands smoothed the floors and walls and put the touch of civilization over the foundation of nature." She sighs and sweeps a hand over the corridor with its columns and frescoes. "But looking at it now, it doesn't look like something that we would have created. I spent all my life amongst the old temples hidden deep within the Frostwood, and... it's just fundamentally different in a way that I can't quite put into words." Hm... "Were we the ones that changed during our exile in the woods? Were the adherents of the human goddess the ones to transform the palace so completely and utterly? Or did the change begin even before the Godswar? I don't know — just staying here's raised so many questions that I'd never taken the time to consider before. I wonder if Elthara would think the same way if she were to visit us for a spell." That remains to be seen. On one hand, Elthara's hard-headed. On the other hand, Hethia's living proof that hard-headedness doesn't necessarily mean being unable to change one's views in light of new evidence and perspectives. You'll have to see how things shake out, but it isn't a lost cause. ] ] "

rows.original: [var0 |[rand |"I... to be honest, when I suggested the whole Xadaron Temple thing, I didn't imagine it'd pay off this well. Mie obviously had a soft spot for her granddad, having been raised on stories of him, but I'd have expected the rest of them to push back a bit harder. For everyone to become a whole lot more reasonable just like that... it's kind of crazy." Was it? As you understood it, the realization that the corrupted wyld trees might not all be dead but instead biding their time might have instilled a sense of urgency in even the most stubborn of the archdruid's colleagues. "It's more the younger ones about Mie's age that're still opposed to the final agreement — the elder druids are like our remaining wyld tree, tired of it all and want to see things done before their time is up. That's a sentiment I'm beginning to respect more and more these days. "Either way, you don't have to worry about it. I'm sure a couple of years spent rebuilding the temple village will mellow them out, hard work has a habit of doing that." Are they going to rebuild Xadaron Temple? From the report, the valkyries caved in the old one during their clean-up so the ground would be more stable and suited to building. "Mmm, there's no reason to, really. The great temples were built to house the wyld trees, and this one's gone; we druids may remain as magicians and artisans, amongst other things, but we're no longer to be purveyors of faith." Hethia sighs and slowly shakes her head, as if she herself can't quite believe it. "The ley-line's still there, so I suppose something may be built there in the future, just not a temple." The future is bright, isn't it? "I don't know if that was meant to be a pun for that sun goddess, but yes, things are looking up from when I was dealing with a bunch of loggers on the other side of the River Ridell." |So, you've been wondering... "Yes?" After all that you've been through together and the way events have shaken out, can you ask her a question? "That depends on what it is. Ask." Back in the Old Forest, when she was, uh, dealing with those loggers... what was that thing that they were getting too close to that she wouldn't tell you or them about? Hethia raises an eyebrow. "You're still thinking about that?" It's what sparked off this lovely relationship that led to this point, after all. If she hadn't been there... if you hadn't been there... would you be here today? Surely now that the druids are letting go of their past and finding a new, more secular role within boreal elf society, perhaps she could tell a friend what that was all about? "I...guess. After what you've done for us, it's not right to treat you like an outsider any longer." Hethia thinks a moment. "The loggers were getting pretty close to one of the burial barrows of one of the archdruids dating from before the Godswar. It was a bothersome situation — if I'd told them what it was, someone would almost certainly go and try to find it. If I told them where to keep away from, that would've given away the general location, and that can be enough to find one of the old burial mounds that've been robbed over the years." And so she saw no choice but to get them to stop altogether, which in turn meant taking their livelihoods away as far as the short term was concerned. But was it so bad, really? One supposes someone in her position couldn't have trusted loggers she met mere days ago. "It's always more complicated than it appears at first glance." No doubt. "But now you know. Happy?" Actually? Yes. Now you have a beginning and an end, or at least where your involvement in this tale is concerned. Thanks. "Don't mention it." |"I wish I could've been with you while you were exploring Xadaron Temple. The things that you saw..." Would likely have revulsed her even more than you did them. And with her druidic magics being completely ineffective against the dangers the infested temple held, she would've been a burden even if she didn't immediately wind up infected with her first breath of spores. Oh gods, the spores, you still remember them — thick and choking, getting into all your cracks and corners. It she wants your honest opinion, it's better that she keeps her mental image of the glory of the druids, rather than see quiet literally how far they fell." Hethia swallows hard. "I guess you're right. Hearing you tell it, I'm not sure how I would've reacted to the corrupted wyld tree. That kind of betrayal, even if she was corrupted... were the Wraiths so powerful that they could have twisted her mind to such a degree? Did she always have a seed of malice that just needed the opportunity to sprout?" The way the wyld tree spoke to you, you get the impression that she saw infesting all the druids with the fungal infection as merely sharing a good thing with them, whether they liked it or not. "That's just as bad in a different way. If the Wraiths could make us perceive evil as good by just tilting the lens a little..." Hethia pauses mid-sentence and shakes her head. "You know what? You're right — even if I were somehow made impervious to infection by that fungus, I wouldn't want to have followed you down into the temple. It would've still been a learning experience, but the cost wouldn't have been worth it." |So, how are her colleagues taking the whole agreement thing? Before, the impression you got was that the talks could've taken years if they'd seriously dragged out; for something this important, even shorter-lived, more impulsive peoples would've taken longer than this, held out for better terms. "Some people do think that we should've done just that, but our wyld tree's already cautioned against demanding a mile after taking an inch. With the archdruid herself having made the call for it herself, no one's going to gainsay the decision already made, so..." What the young complainers need is a year or two getting the old temple village back into shape. Something to spend all their energy on instead of chasing tails. "Some of them aren't too keen on setting off just yet — there's some understandable suspicion that this is a trap of some sort, that the valkyries didn't clear out all of the infectious fungus, that the moment they get too close they'll be infested with Wraith-taint and turned into monsters." Hethia sighs. "It's a little ironic that there's more enthusiasm for the resettlement from the common people of Njorhaalt — even without us adding to the headcount, the city's been getting quite crowded this last decade, or so Elthara tells me. That's one of the reasons why Daliza was sent out to Dracia." When are the first people heading out for the whole resettlement thing, anyway? "Soon enough. It's not just about putting out the call for people, but the palace is also gathering the necessary provisions to supply said settlers for about a year until some kind of self-sufficiency can be achieved. It doesn't have to be all at once, but still the necessary goods needed to embark isn't something to sniff at. The mood of the people has been pretty good ever since Alissa's ouster, so there's no shortage of volunteers, we just have to figure out how to squeeze blood from the proverbial rock of the empty treasury." Good luck with the whole thing. Another sigh. "You know... all this wouldn't have been possible without you, [pc.name]. So I'm going to say it again — thanks for everything you've done." |So, you've been meaning to ask ever since you encountered a wyld tree for yourself: the last uncorrupted wyld tree that still lives, the druids' current patron... Hethia squints at you, reading your expression, then thins her lips at the unspoken question. "She's dying, yes. You know that." You understand that this is blunt, but how long will it take? The one you met in the ruins of Xadaron Temple seemed hale and hearty enough — too hale and hearty, given the nature of her corruption. At the same time, you also figure that the timeline the boreal elves and the wyld trees operate on isn't the same as most other Savarran peoples, so what's soon to them might be considerably longer in absolute terms. "We... we don't know for sure. It could be a year. The tree herself says no more than a decade, she can feel it in her roots. We can only hope that there's enough time for us to be weaned off our old habits and adopt new ones. It's less a physical thing, [pc.name], and more a spiritual one. "I'm not going to deny it, delivering the truth of what'd happened at Xadaron Temple to our patron diminished her will to live considerably. She said... she said she'd always suspected something like that, but had no proof of it. Now she's even more convinced that the time of her and her siblings is now over." You're — Hethia holds out a hand. "We don't want or need your pity or trite apologies. What you did — what I recommended you do — was the right thing, and there's no need to second-guess ourselves, especially after the fact. Our patron herself said that dying knowing the truth is better than living and always wondering, always suspecting... we've made important strides forward towards the future of late, so let's focus on that when there aren't any more lessons to be learned from this bit of past. Just moping around is going to make the parting worse." |So, now that the talks are more or less concluded, what's Hethia going to do from here on out? Is she going to leave with the rest of the druidic delegation? Is she going to help with the rebuilding of Xadaron Temple? "To be frank, I'm not completely sure," Hethia replies, tapping her chin and looking thoughtful. "Elthara's suggested that I stay on at the palace as a liaison, but that decision isn't in my hands. If the archdruid or my elders say that I'm needed somewhere else, I go, no questions asked. "Truth be told, I like it here in the palace. Norathar's getting along great with the other wargs in the kennels, and the creature comforts are very appealing. I can see why the druids of old were very reluctant to give up their station in boer'alvar society of the past." So, she's going to be leaving? "I didn't say anything of the kind, and if it does happen it probably won't be any time soon. I'll be in the palace for the foreseeable future, helping to put together provisions for the resettlement effort and making sure that the terms of the reunification are adhered to — by both sides, of course." Well, you're glad for that. Since Hethia entered the palace about the same time as you did, you've gotten used to her being as much of a fixture as you are, if not more. You aren't the only person who'd miss her if she were to have to pull up her roots. "That's... well, thank you for the compliment. And please be careful out there, especially when you're dragging our dear var Ridell with you. It wouldn't be the same without you around." ] |[hethia.isHostile |[rand |Hethia glares over her shoulder at you. "What does it matter? Once these talks are over, we're going to be effectively disbanded. What would you gain from learning about a soon to be dead way of life? Why would you bother to do such a thing save to mock us?" Because even though the druidic faith of the pale elves may eventually come to be dissolved, the impact it's had on its adherents lingers — the Winter City is proof of that. Even after two and a half centuries after abandoning those ways and practices and the current generation of pale elves having grown up knowing nothing but the worship of Lumia, she can still tell that there's some measure of the Old Wyld in their culture and blood, repurposed as it may be. That sort of thing doesn't wash out in one generation, or two, or six, if ever. That's why it's important for you to understand it while there's still someone around who can explain it effectively to you. Now then, what was the worship of the Old Wyld all about? You've heard a whole lot about it to date, and that the ancient wyld trees of the Frostwood were kind of a stand-in for deities-but-not-quite-deities for this religion-but-not-quite-religion, but what exactly are its tenets and precepts, anyway? Even if she can't fully explain it to you — and you don't expect to perfectly comprehend it, either — you'd appreciate it if she made the attempt. Hethia coughs. Why, does she still not want to tell you? It can't be helped if she's still not convinced, but — "No, no, I'll tell you about us and our beliefs, to get you off my back if nothing else. "I suppose you could call it a form of animism. That there are powers in objects, places and living things, and sometimes these manifest with intelligence and personality. When the boer'alvar ranged throughout the Frostwood, the druidic circles mostly busied ourselves with negotiating a reasonable coexistence between us and the powers present in the Frostwood, such that we might take what we needed and traverse its glades and trails safely, that we could build under the pine canopy so long as we kept spaces within artifice for the natural world. "The wyld trees are not gods as someone from the south would understand the term — while powerful, they certainly do not approach omnipotence, and their reach only extends to the Frostwood and to a lesser extent, the lands you know as the Old Forest. Yet within their domain, they hold much sway, and were eager to serve as a collective memory of sorts for the boer'alvar in exchange for being enshrined, cared for, and some might say, worshipped. Certainly, while many druids drew power from the spirits of the forests and fjords, the wyld trees were first and foremost amongst these animistic entities, and granted magics and powers to those who were faithful to them." You see. "I don't think we actually had any true precepts, not in the way that those who worship the southern gods do. It was a closer, more personal relationship where we interacted with the wyld trees every day and could converse with them directly if we had the mind to. There weren't any clever interpretations of what they really meant, because anyone could simply go up and ask the wyld trees of their intentions — each and every one of them had a link of sorts, where if one of them knew something, the rest would, too. When the Godswar first came upon our borders, the winter city knew of it almost immediately after it began..." You're starting to see where this is headed. Small-scale religion of sorts, each with their own customs in accordance with the local wyld tree's quirks and desires; beliefs focused on mediation with the natural world, and by and large a fairly loose hierarchy in which individuals were given a lot of leeway to do as they wished with the sensibilities of the people they served taken into accord as opposed to universal standards. While you're sure there's a lot of nuance, Hethia's at least given you something to start with, and that's good. A disdainful snort. "We'll see about that; I still don't expect someone like you to understand. It's one thing to live it, [pc.name], and another to try and put it into words for someone who might not find it all immediately obvious." |You're given to understand that the pale elf druids were guardians of the forest of sorts, then. Certainly she mentioned during the audience with Ryn that the whole reason she went after Westbank was because their logging operations were encroaching upon one of the remaining wyld trees. "I suppose you think it stupid, then," Hethia says with a sniff. "I had to tell them to stay away, yet wouldn't tell them where they needed to stay away from." Well, it's not so much stupid as she was caught between conflicting demands of her beliefs and allegiances. While an unpleasant situation for anyone to find themselves in, it's not as if it's a situation that's unique to her and hers. "Ever so carefully diplomatic, I see." This is a diplomatic matter, of course you should be diplomatic. There's a begrudging silence, and at last Hethia shrugs. "I guess you could've called us that, yes. None of that whole dancing in the woods naked nonsense to 'reconnect with your roots' — that's just trash that [pc.ra elf |wyld elves like you |wyld elves ] spout when they go back into the woods to have an excuse to fuck around, and other peoples can't tell the difference between one stripe of elf and another. As far as our so-called guardianship of the forest went about, it was about interacting with the numerous minor spirits that make up the forests and fjords; within the domain of the Frostwood, the wyld trees might have been the greatest and most prominent amongst them, but all lands are possessed of a bewildering array of minor spirits and entities whom we as the boer'alvar needed to entreat with in our daily lives. The whole 'guardian of the forest' thing is true inasmuch as if the land is damaged, its spirits are, too; hence, we were charged with preventing that from happening." See, things are so much clearer and unpleasantness so easily avoided if she would just explain things. "Should they become angered, we were summoned to address the source of that anger and placate them, resolve the root of the problem at hand; as we lived in the Frostwood at the time, what perturbed them would also perturb us. It was a symbiotic relationship of sorts... as druids, we were able to interact better with the world than the spirits of the forests and fjords were, especially upon the fringes of or outside their domains, and in turn we drew power from them. Before the arrival of the southern goddess Lumia, these spirits were always on the fringes of our lives, and once sin, incompetence and cruelty reared their heads amongst the boer'alvar they would be angered and lead them to punish or torment said people until the spirits were placated." It sounds like they were more guardians of the people than guardians of the forest. Hethia purses her lips. "More mediators than anything else. But then, I wouldn't expect even a boer'alvar of the Winter City to understand, let alone someone like you, so you can't be blamed for your ignorance — it requires one to draw upon a frame of reference that you simply don't have." |What exactly are the wyld trees, anyway? Are they the gods that the druids worship? Hethia scowls. "Of course you'd make that mistake. No, the wyld trees aren't gods in the way that you would understand them, like these Seven that all of the world now pays reverence to. They are powerful, yes, they are spiritual in nature, but I would hesitate to call them gods. They are just very, very old trees who have been tended to by generations of druids, and remember things very well. When you get to that kind of stage and accumulate that kind of power within yourself, it's conceivable that one might be mistaken for a deity, but no... they are powerful spirits that are aware of their own limitations and have no such delusions of grandeur. Consider them merely very ancient grandparents that you might have, capable and wise, but still approachable and relatable should you make the effort." The pale elves built temples to them, though. They worshipped them, and the druids served much the same purpose as the Lumian priests do now in pale elf society. While you can accept that they might be different in essence and nature, practically as they are — correction, were — to the pale elves they may as well have been gods. Hethia sniffs. "I suppose I can't say that you're wrong, but it's more like respecting and acknowledging your grandmother's power and prowess than any kind of divine reverence. The acknowledgement that they're older, wiser and more worldly than you are, if nothing else. The difference is important." And some people engage in ancestor worship. But yes, you think you see the point. "It's undeniable that your gods exist, [pc.name]. I can't just set aside the evidence of my own eyes, not when they're walking around and granting small miracles to their worshippers every day. But there are other spiritual powers in Savarra that aren't them and aren't gods in the same way that they are, and some of those have accumulated considerable power over time. The wyld trees fall into that category. And now those who did not pass in the Godswar have accepted their passing at the hands of time, for all good that their immortality has done them." ... "If you accumulate enough power, you might become something like them. If anyone did, to be honest. It's getting to that point that's the tricky part." |"We used to produce much of the wine that the boer'alvar drank. It was, and still is a point of pride for us — one of the first things I did was to go down into the palace's wine cellars and see how well-stocked they were after more than two centuries. I must say, I'm rather pleased." Is that right? You've seen some of the vintages served here in the palace of ice, and you always wondered. But could the wine have lasted that long? Hethia sneers. "While the var Ridell line predictably descended into worthless debauchery and their appetites were massive, so were the reserves the palace had in store. More than two hundred years of use, and they were only a little under half full." Huh. the pale elves must have really loved their wine... "Mirrorwine, or ice wine as it's more commonly known to other peoples, is made from more than just grapes; it's a careful blend of [silly |eleven secret berries, herbs and spices |various fruits and herbs ] that've been cultivated for many generations by the druids. In times past, there was considerable pressure for us to produce as much as possible, but we always stuck to the yearly quotas before telling the crown no more. It was how we earned respect in the eyes of the common boer'alvar, to show that we weren't afraid of getting our hands dirty when need be." And there's no magic in the wine or the vinting process? The sneer widens. "No, we don't cheat. The frostmander princes used to say it must have been, but no, there's nothing magical about the vinting process, or mystical secret ingredients involved in its making; both hows and whos alike have just been refined and perfected over a long, long time. Mirrorwine is a symbol of culture, of spirituality, of careful stewardship of the Wyld, and now that things are changing, it will likely take on new, but similar meanings." She sounds a lot less bitter about this than the other aspects of her religion fading away... "Bitter as I may be, I think we can all agree that Mirrorwine is something that should not vanish from the face of Savarra. Even if it loses its meaning, its taste alone carries with it the memories of its past; as much as I think the Winter City doesn't deserve to have the secrets of its making, we are all given boons we don't deserve every day. Deserve has nothing to do with it, as the saying goes." |"What's the point?" Come again? "I mean it. Why are you even bothering to ask this question? We're dying. We'll soon be dead. All these negotiations with the Winter City are merely making arrangements to commit at least a somewhat dignified suicide instead of wasting away over the next two or three decades — tying up all the loose ends so that at least we schismatics aren't left to rot when the dust blows over. It's dressed up in pretty words and sweet gestures, but I know Elthara's hiding a stupid smirk every time she sits down on the opposite end of the table. She and her ilk have won, and she knows it." Look, maybe she's sounding a little bitter, but — "Bitter? Of course I'm bitter. Why shouldn't I be bitter? The realization that all of my life, all of our lives working away to stave off this end, or something like it, has been meaningless and I might as well have spent my time doing something else? You resent me for taking those loggers hostage — well, that has also been made meaningless by this. Nothing's changed, the end for the Old Wyld and its druidic circles still looms, and the only choice left to us is how we want to die, rather than the choice to die at all. That sense of meaningless nothingness — wouldn't you be bitter at the sense of cosmic injustice, too?" See, if she'd let you get in a word edgewise, the point is that it doesn't have to be a waste. Whether she feels this ending that has been forced upon her by the ancients has made the struggle of her life meaningless, what she feels and what's real aren't necessarily the same. It's a bad situation, but her experiences have — " "Just shut up already, I don't need your silver-lining-on-the-cloud make-the-best-out-of-a-bad-situation pandering in the least." Damn it, you're just trying to help her help herself, she's acting like a child here. "If you don't want a hostile response then don't treat people like idiots and helpfully point out the obvious! This entire exercise is an attempt to make the best of a bad situation; you're telling me to do what I'm already doing, hence giving me worthless advice! Think before you flap your lips and make meaningless noises!" You consider a rebuttal, then realize that here and now, Hethia doesn't want solutions — she just wants to be mad, and anything you say is going to be pounced on as a pretext to get even angrier than she already is. At this point, disengaging, or at least changing the subject would be par for the course because there's no way to make any kind of inroad at this point. ] |[rand |"Time used to be when the boer'alvar ranged across the entirety of the Frostwood. Its length and breadth was alive with the voices of people, and we druids oversaw them as agents of the crown, official and unofficial alike, ensured that they walked with the Wyld." It must be something, to hear stories of such a time while sitting in its ruins. Does she ever wish she could have experienced that golden age for herself? Hethia shakes her head. "Tempting, but no. It would have its merits, but that era of our history was also too peaceful for the likes of someone like me. The stories are nice, but I'm one more for conflict, and this age of the boer'alvar need those like me." The stories... "Yes, the stories. Anyone can easily see for themselves that they're not cooked up from simple nostalgia — the Frostwood is rife with elven ruins all the way down to the river by the south." That's right, you've had to pass the Wayfort and the adjoining old stone bridge on your way up to the Winter City. It was where you met Ryn, after all. "That Wayfort used to garrison anywhere from between thirty to fifty outriders and their mounts; the bridge and river marked the border between lands claimed by the boer'alvar and the lupine tribes, the latter of which later was consumed by the Belharan Empire. It was the first of the outposts to fall when the troubles began..." Then for as much to remain as it has, the worksmanship must have been something in its heyday. "By your standards, our buildings last well. By our standards, they are annoying things that constantly demand maintenance every decade or so," Hethia replies with a thin smile. "But since the end of the Godswar and the resultant schism in our people, there was no need to maintain the Wayfort, nor any of the outrider outposts in the Frostwood." The outriders no longer existed? "Oh, a good number survived the fighting, that's for sure, and they still continued to patrol the Frostwood. But where they once did so to keep the trails and paths safe from the forest's more unfriendly denizens and other darker creatures from beyond, now they did it to keep the Winter City safe from us. Atheldred was not unreasonably concerned that we wouldn't be content in our exile, self-imposed as it was... and to be fair, the early years saw several calls for and a handful of isolated incidents of surreptitious strikes against the people who had rejected us, who had embraced this new, foreign goddess." ... "None of them ever did much good, of course, and after a few run-ins with the outriders and several unfortunate deaths things just stopped. Even after all this, no one really wanted to pit sister against sister." Hethia sighs. "For a couple of centuries, the outsiders made cursory patrols of the Frostwood's fringes; we'd ignore them, and they'd ignore us. And then, a couple decades ago, they stopped coming altogether." If you remember right, that should have been around when Alissa took the throne... which makes perfect sense. She'd have seen no need to continue the patrols, seeing them as a waste of resources that could've been frittered away in decadence. "And when the outriders departed then it was just us, in the ruins of what used to be our glory." Hethia finishes with a sigh. "Born too early to see the schism mended, too late to have enjoyed any of the glories while they lasted — and just in time to fight tooth and nail for our future. What a time to be alive." |What exactly are the wyld trees, anyway? Are they the gods that the druids worship? "Not gods in the way that you would understand them, like these Seven that all of the world now pays reverence to. They are powerful, yes, they are spiritual in nature, but I would hesitate to call them gods. They are just very, very old trees who have been tended to by generations of druids, and remember things very well. When you get to that kind of stage and accumulate that kind of power, it's conceivable that one might be mistaken for a deity, but no... they are powerful spirits that are aware of their own limitations and have no such delusions of grandeur. Consider them merely very ancient grandparents that you might have." The pale elves built temples to them, though. They worshipped them, and the druids served much the same purpose as the Lumian priests do now in pale elf society. While you can accept that they might be different in essence and nature, practically as they are — correction, were — to the pale elves they may as well have been gods. Hethia mulls over that for a moment. "I suppose I can't say that you're wrong, but it's more like respecting and acknowledging your grandmother's power and prowess than any kind of divine reverence. The acknowledgement that they're older, wiser and more worldly than you are, if nothing else." And some people engage in ancestor worship. But yes, you think you see the point. "It's undeniable that your gods exist, [pc.name]. No one's claiming that, not when they're walking around and granting small miracles to their worshippers every day. But there are other spiritual powers in Savarra that aren't them and aren't gods in the same way that they are, and some of those have accumulated considerable power over time. The wyld trees fall into that category. And now those who did not pass in the Godswar have accepted their passing at the hands of time, for all good that their immortality has done them." ... "If you accumulate enough power, you might become something like them. If anyone did, to be honest. It's getting to that point that's the tricky part." |How did the druids make a living in the Frostwood? You're guessing that they didn't farm in the commonly accepted sense, but did they just use their powers to make fruit fall from the bough, or... "By the Wyld, not that kind of nonsense, none of it at all! That's just trash that [pc.ra elf |wyld elves who're less scrupulous than you |wyld elves ] spout when they go back into the woods to 'reconnect with their roots', as it were. No, there was a lot of work involved in being a druid back in the day, and we tried to keep some of them alive. For example, before the schism, our vineyards were simply the best to be had; mirrorwine — or ice wine, as it was known outside our lands — was popularised when a frostmander prince took a liking to it. Not that we had much use for the glass doodads his principality was famous for, but it brought the Winter City some prestige." And is it still being made now? "A little. The regent tells me that the crown has tried to recreate it without the druids, but they've never managed to get it quite right." Hethia allows herself a little smirk. "But yes, back to your question — even in our heyday our duties involved a lot of work, a good deal of it dirty, tiring and even dangerous. Things have only grown more desperate since then." |"We used to produce much of the wine that the boer'alvar drank." Is that right? You've seen some of the vintages served here in the palace of ice, and you always wondered. But could the wine have lasted that long? "I made a cursory tour of the wine cellars shortly after I settled in my quarters — while the former queen's appetites were massive, so were the reserves the palace had in store. More than two hundred years of use, and they were only a little under half full." Huh. the pale elves must have really loved their wine... "Mirrorwine, or ice wine as it's more commonly known to other peoples, is made from more than just grapes; it's a careful blend of [silly |eleven secret berries, herbs and spices |various fruits and herbs ] that've been cultivated for many generations by the druids. In times past, there was considerable pressure for us to produce as much as possible, but we always stuck to the yearly quotas before telling the crown no more. It was how we earned respect in the eyes of the common boer'alvar, to show that we weren't afraid of getting our hands dirty when need be." And there's no magic in it? Hethia laughs. "The frostmander princes used to say it must have been, but no, there's nothing magical about the vinting process, or mystical secret ingredients involved in its making; both hows and whos alike have just been refined and perfected over a long, long time. Mirrorwine is a symbol of culture, of spirituality, of careful stewardship of the Wyld, and now that things are changing, it will likely take on new, but similar meanings." She sounds a lot less bitter about this than the other aspects of her religion fading away... "Bitter as I may be, I think we can all agree that Mirrorwine is something that should not vanish from the face of Savarra. Even if it loses its meaning, its taste alone carries with it the memories of its past." |So, what was the worship of the Old Wyld all about? You've heard a whole lot about it to date, and that the ancient wyld trees of the Frostwood were kind of a stand-in for deities-but-not-quite-deities for this religion-but-not-quite-religion, but what exactly are its tenets and precepts, anyway? "I know you don't mean malice, [pc.name], but even so it can be a little hard to speak of a religion that's dying before your eyes. Give me a moment to gather myself, please, and then I'll elaborate." Oh, of course. Even if she can't fully explain it to you — and you don't expect to perfectly comprehend it, either — you'd appreciate it if she made the attempt. "I suppose you could call it a form of animism. That there are powers in objects, places and living things, and sometimes these manifest with intelligence and personality. When the boer'alvar ranged throughout the Frostwood, the druidic circles mostly busied ourselves with negotiating a reasonable coexistence between us and the powers present in the Frostwood, such that we might take what we needed and traverse its glades and trails safely, that we could build under the pine canopy so long as we kept spaces within artifice for the natural world. "The wyld trees are not gods as someone from the south would understand the term — while powerful, they certainly do not approach omnipotence, and their reach only extends to the Frostwood and to a lesser extent, the lands you know as the Old Forest. Yet within their domain, they hold much sway, and were eager to serve as a collective memory of sorts for the boer'alvar in exchange for being enshrined, cared for, and some might say, worshipped. Certainly, while many druids drew power from the spirits of the forests and fjords, the wyld trees were first and foremost amongst these animistic entities, and granted magics and powers to those who were faithful to them." You see. "I don't think we actually had any true precepts, not in the way that those who worship the southern gods do. It was a closer, more personal relationship where we interacted with the wyld trees every day and could converse with them directly if we had the mind to. There weren't any clever interpretations of what they really meant, because anyone could simply go up and ask the wyld trees of their intentions — each and every one of them had a link of sorts, where if one of them knew something, the rest would, too. When the Godswar first came upon our borders, the winter city knew of it almost immediately after it began..." You're starting to see where this is headed. Small-scale religion of sorts, each with their own customs in accordance with the local wyld tree's quirks and desires; beliefs focused on mediation with the natural world, and by and large a fairly loose hierarchy in which individuals were given a lot of leeway to do as they wished with the sensibilities of the people they served taken into accord as opposed to universal standards. While you're sure there's a lot of nuance, Hethia's at least given you something to start with, and that's good. A rueful smile. "It's one thing to live it, [pc.name], and another to try and put it into words for someone who might not find it all immediately obvious." ] ] ]
rows.translation: [var0 |[rand |说实话，当我提出建立Xadaron神庙这个想法时，根本没预料到它会取得这么好的效果。Mie显然对她的祖父情有独钟，因为她从小就听着关于他的故事长大，但我原本以为其他人的反应会更强烈一些。没想到所有人都突然变得如此通情达理……这简直太不可思议了。 真是这样吗？正如你所理解的那样，当人们意识到那些被腐蚀的野生树木可能并没有全部死亡，而是在等待时机时，就连最固执的大德鲁伊的同事们也感受到了紧迫感。 主要是那些与米耶年龄相仿的年轻德鲁伊们仍然反对这项最终协议——而那些年长的德鲁伊们，就如同我们仅存的‘荒野之树’一样，已经对这一切感到厌倦，他们希望在自己有生之年内看到这些事情得到解决。这种想法，这些天来，我越来越感到敬重了。 无论如何，你都不必担心这个。我相信，花上几年时间重建寺庙村庄，一定能让他们冷静下来——努力工作总是会有这样的效果。” 他们是要重建Xadaron寺庙吗？从报告来看，女武神们在清理旧寺庙时使其倒塌了，这样地基就会更加稳固，更适合重建了。 嗯，其实也没必要这样吧。那些伟大的神庙本来就是为安置那些野生树木而建造的，而现在的那棵树已经不见了；我们德鲁伊或许还可以继续担任魔法师、工匠等等角色，但我们已经不再是为人们提供信仰指引的存在了。”赫希娅叹了口气，缓缓摇了摇头，似乎她自己也不太能相信这一点。“那条能量脉络依然存在，所以我想将来或许还是可以在那里建造些什么，只不过不会再是神庙了。 未来一片光明，不是吗？ “我不知道这是否是在故意模仿那位太阳女神的名字，但确实，自从我在里德尔河对岸与那些伐木工们打交道之后，情况确实有所好转。 |所以，你一直在思考…… “是吗？” 经历了这么多一起度过的时光，也看着种种事情逐渐发展成现在的样子，你现在真的可以问她那个问题了吗？ “这得看那个问题是什么。 问吧。” 回到那片古老的森林里，当时她正在对付那些伐木工……有没有什么事情，因为他们靠得太近了，所以她既不愿意告诉你，也不愿意告诉他们？ 赫希娅挑了挑眉毛。 你还在想着那件事吗？” 毕竟，正是这件事促成了我们这段美好的关系，让我们走到了今天这一步。如果她当时没有出现在我的身边……如果 你 如果我当时不在那里……你现在还会在这里吗？既然德鲁伊们已经放下了过去的包袱，在北方精灵社会中找到了新的、更为世俗的角色，或许她可以向朋友解释这一切到底意味着什么吧？ 我……想应该是这样。既然你为我们做了这么多，再把你当作外人对待就不对了。”赫希娅思考了一会儿，继续说道：“那些伐木工人们已经快要挖到那些远古大祭司在神战之前建造的墓葬了。 这确实是个令人烦恼的情况——要是我当初告诉了他们的话 什么 肯定有人会去尝试寻找它。如果我告诉他们应该避开哪些地方，那就等于暴露了它的大致位置，而这样一来，那些这些年来被盗过的古老墓葬就很容易被找到了。因此，她别无选择，只能让他们彻底停止这些活动。而从短期来看，这意味着要剥夺他们的生计。但真的有那么糟糕吗？想来，处于她这种境地的人，肯定不会信任那些仅仅几天前才认识的山林伐木工人们。 事情总是比乍看之下要复杂得多。” 毫无疑问。 “但现在你知道了。开心吗？” 其实吧？挺开心的。现在你终于知道了事情的起因和结局，至少对于你在这个故事中的角色而言是这样。 不用谢。 |真希望你在探索扎达隆神庙的时候能在你身边。你所看到的一切……” 那些景象很可能也会让她感到极度厌恶，甚至比你感受到的还要强烈。更何况，她的德鲁伊魔法对那座充满危险的神庙完全无效，如果她没有在吸入第一缕孢子时就立刻被感染，她反而会成为你的负担。 哦，天啊，那些孢子……你们应该还记得吧——它们又浓又黏，会钻进你身体的每一个缝隙里。如果她真的想听到你的真实看法，那么她最好继续保持着自己对德鲁伊们昔日辉煌的想象，而不是亲眼看到他们如今已经堕落到了什么地步。" 赫希娅艰难地咽了口唾沫，说道：“我想你是对的。听你这么一说，我也不知道自己遇到那棵被腐蚀的野树时会做出什么反应。那样的背叛……即使她已经被腐蚀了……那些幽灵的力量真的有那么大，能够彻底扭曲她的思想吗？还是说，她内心本来就藏着恶意，只是需要机会才会爆发出来呢？ 当那棵野生树木与你交流时，你会觉得，它将那种真菌感染传播给所有德鲁伊，仅仅被视为是在与他们分享一些有益的东西而已，无论他们是否愿意接受这些“礼物”。 “从另一个角度来看，这也同样糟糕。 如果那些幽灵能够稍微改变我们的认知角度，让我们把邪恶看作是善良……”赫希娅话说到一半停了下来，摇了摇头。“你知道吗？你说得对——即使我因为某种原因对那种真菌产生了免疫力，我也不会愿意跟着你进入那座寺庙的。 那仍然会是一次学习经历，但所付出的代价显然不值得。 |那么，她的同事们对这项协议究竟有什么看法呢？之前给人的感觉是，如果谈判真的拖得那么久，的话，可能要花费好几年的时间；对于这么重要的事情来说，即使是那些性格更为急躁、做事更缺乏耐心的人，也会花更长的时间来争取更好的条件。 “有些人 做 我认为我们本应该那么做的，但我们的“荒野之树”早就提醒过我们，不要得寸进尺。既然大德鲁伊本人已经做出了这个决定，那么没有人会反对这个已经做出的选择，所以……那些爱抱怨的年轻人所需要的，就是花一两年时间把那个古老的寺庙村庄重新整顿好。这样他们就可以把所有的精力都投入到这项工作中，而不是浪费在无谓的争吵上。” “其中有些人还不太愿意立刻动身——他们自然会怀疑这其实是一个陷阱，怀疑那些女武神并没有真正清除那里的危险。 所有 那种具有传染性的真菌，一旦人们靠得太近，就会被‘幽灵污染’侵蚀，进而变成怪物。”赫希娅叹道，“有点讽刺的是，尼乔哈尔特的普通民众对重新安置计划表现得格外热情——据埃尔萨拉说，即使在没有我们增加人口数量的情况下，这座城市在过去的十年里也变得相当拥挤了。 这就是为什么达丽莎被派往德拉西亚的原因之一。” 那么，第一批进行重新安置的人什么时候出发呢？ “很快就会出发。我们不仅仅是在招募人员，宫廷还在准备必要的物资，以便为这些移民提供大约一年的生活保障，直到他们能够实现自给自足为止。 这些物资并不一定需要一次性全部准备到位，但那些出发旅行所必需的物品数量确实不容小觑。自从艾丽莎被罢免之后，人们的情绪一直相当积极，因此志愿者也不缺，我们只需要想办法从那几乎空无一物的国库中挤出一些资金来罢了。祝你在整个过程中一切顺利。 又一声叹息：“你知道……如果没有你，这一切都不可能实现。 [pc.name]所以，我还是要再说一遍——感谢你们所做的一切。 |所以，自从你亲眼见到那棵最后的、尚未被腐蚀的野生树木以来，你就一直想问这个问题：那棵至今依然存活着的、德鲁伊们目前所依赖的守护树…… 赫希娅眯起眼睛，仔细观察你的表情，然后针对你未说出口的疑问轻声说道：“她确实快不行了。你应该知道的。” 你明白她的回答很直白，但这个过程到底还需要多久呢？你在扎达隆神庙的废墟里遇到的那棵树，看起来可是一点毛病都没有啊 太 考虑到她所经历的那些变故，她依然显得精神矍铄、身体健康。同时，你也应该明白：极北精灵与那些野生树木所遵循的时间流逝规律，与其他大多数萨瓦兰民族是不同的。因此，对他们来说很快发生的事情，在绝对时间尺度上，可能会持续相当长的时间。 我们……我们也不能确定。可能需要一年的时间。那棵树本身也只表示不超过十年的时间，它从自己的根部感受到了这一点。我们只能希望有足够的时间让我们改掉旧习惯，养成新的习惯。 这与其说是一种物理上的东西，不如说 [pc.name]更确切地说，这是一种精神上的打击。 “我不得不承认，将发生在扎达伦神庙里的真相告诉我们的赞助人，确实使她的生存意志受到了极大的打击。她说……她说她一直以来都怀疑会发生这样的事情，但却没有任何证据。 现在，她更加确信，她和她的兄弟姐妹们的时代已经结束了。 你—— 赫希娅伸出了手部：“我们不需要你的同情，也不需要那些老套的道歉。你所做的——也就是我建议你去做的——才是正确的做法，根本没有必要事后自我怀疑。 我们的赞助人本人也说过，明知真相而死去，总比活着一直充满疑惑、一直心存怀疑要好……最近，我们在迈向未来的道路上取得了重要的进展，所以当这段过去不再能给我们带来任何启示时，让我们把注意力放在未来吧。 只是闷闷不乐地待着，只会让分别变得更加难熬。 |那么，既然谈判已经基本结束，赫希娅接下来会做什么呢？她是会和其他德鲁伊代表团成员一起离开，还是会帮忙重建扎达伦神庙呢？ 说实话，我并不是完全确定，”赫希娅托着下巴，若有所思地回答道，“埃尔萨拉建议我留在宫殿里担任联络人，但这个决定并不由我来做。如果大德鲁伊或者我的长辈们认为我需要去别的地方，那我就会去，没有任何疑问。 说实话，我挺喜欢在宫殿里生活的。诺拉萨尔和其他那些狼族相处得很好，而且这里的生活条件也非常舒适。我能够理解为什么过去的德鲁伊们如此不愿意放弃他们在博尔阿尔瓦尔社会中的地位。 所以，她要离开了吗？ “我并没有说过那样的话，而且如果真发生了，恐怕也不会很快。在可预见的未来，我都会留在宫殿里，协助准备重新安置的相关工作，确保双方都能遵守重新统一的各项条款。 嗯，你为此感到庆幸吧。既然赫希娅和你差不多同时进入宫殿的，你早就已经习惯了她成为这里不可或缺的一部分——甚至可以说，她的地位比你还要重要。如果她真的不得不离开这里，不止你会想念她。 那……嗯，谢谢你的夸奖。不过在外面请一定要小心，尤其是当你带着我们亲爱的拉·里德尔一起行动的时候。没有你的话，事情就不会像现在这样顺利了。 ] |[hethia.isHostile |[rand |赫希娅回头瞪了你一眼，说道：“这有什么关系呢？等这些谈判结束，我们实际上就已经解散了。了解一种即将消失的生活方式，你能得到什么好处呢？你为什么要费心去做这种事，只不过是为了嘲笑我们罢了。因为尽管苍白精灵的德鲁伊信仰最终可能会消亡，但它对信徒们所产生的影响依然存在——冬城就是明证。即使在放弃了那些信仰与习俗两个半世纪之后，当代的苍白精灵们自幼只知道崇拜卢米娅，她仍然能够感觉到，他们的文化与血液中依然流淌着某种古老的野性，尽管这些元素已经被赋予了新的含义。 这种影响不会在一代人、两代人，甚至六代人的时间里消失，甚至可能永远都不会消失。 那就是。 为什么在还有别人能够有效地为你解释这些内容的时候，你理解它们是如此重要呢？ 那么，接下来是什么呢？ 是 关于这种对“古老荒野”的崇拜，你肯定已经听了很多。据说，在这种宗教中，弗罗斯特伍德的那些古老荒野之树某种程度上被视为神明，但又不完全是神明；这种信仰也算是一种宗教，但又不完全是宗教。那么，它的具体信条和准则究竟是什么呢？即使她无法完全向你解释清楚——其实你也不期望她能完全理解这些内容——但如果你她能尝试去解释，你也会感到很感激的。 赫希娅轻咳了一声。 “为什么，她还是不愿意告诉你吗？如果她还没有被说服的话，那也没办法……但是——” “不，不，我一定会告诉你关于我们以及我们的信仰的事情，至少这样就能让你不再纠缠我了。 不过，苍白的精灵们还是为它们建造了寺庙。 他们崇拜这些存在，而德鲁伊们所扮演的角色，与如今苍白精灵社会中卢米安祭司的角色几乎相同。虽然你可以认为它们在本质和性质上可能存在差异，但实际上……嗯，应该说是，它们的功能是相同的。 是 — 对那些苍白的精灵们来说，他们简直就像神明一般。 赫希娅沉思了一会儿，说道：“我想我不能说你错了，但这种态度更像是对你祖母的力量和能力的尊重与认可，而非真正的神明崇拜。 至少，他们承认自己比你年长、更有智慧，也更加阅历丰富。 当然，也有些人会崇拜祖先。不过，嗯，你大概也能理解其中的原因吧。 不可否认，你们的神灵确实是存在的。 [pc.name]没有人会这么声称，尤其是当他们每天都在四处走动，为他们的信徒们创造种种奇迹的时候。但在萨瓦拉，还有其他的灵力存在，它们并非神明，也不具备与他们相同的性质；其中一些灵力随着时间的推移，已经积累了相当强大的力量。 那些野生的树木也属于这一类。而如今，那些在“神战”中未能存活下来的人，也已经接受了时间带来的终结……尽管他们的永生曾给他们带来过许多好处。如果你积累了足够的力量，或许也能变成他们那样的存在。如果 有人吗？ 说实话，确实到了那个地步，而这正是最棘手部的地方。 |德鲁伊们在霜林里是如何谋生的呢？你可能会猜他们并不是以我们通常理解的方式从事农业，但难道他们只是利用自己的力量让果实从树枝上掉落，还是…… “看在荒野之神的份上，绝对不是那种无聊的事情，完全不是！那些只是无稽之谈罢了 [pc.ra elf |那些比你更肆无忌惮的野精灵们 |野生精灵 ] 当他们回到森林中，试图“与自己的根源重新建立联系”时，其实需要付出很多努力。在古代，成为一名德鲁伊确实需要承担许多责任，我们也尽力让其中的一些传统得以延续。例如，在教派分裂之前，我们的葡萄园绝对是最好的；而镜像酒——在我们以外的地区，人们称之为冰酒——之所以能够流行起来，也是因为有一位霜冻领主王子非常喜欢这种酒。 虽然我们对他那个公国闻名的玻璃制品并没有太大需求，但它们确实为冬城带来了一些声望。 那么，现在还在生产这些制品吗？ “还有少量在生产。 摄政王告诉我，王室曾经尝试过在没有德鲁伊的帮助下重新创造它，但他们始终无法做到完美。”赫希娅微微一笑，“不过，回到你的问题上来——即使在我们最鼎盛的时期，我们的职责也意味着大量的工作，其中很多工作既繁琐又辛苦，甚至充满危险。 从那以后，情况只会变得更加糟糕。 |我们曾经生产过布尔阿尔瓦人饮用的大部分葡萄酒。” 真的是这样吗？你在冰之宫殿里品尝过这里提供的那些葡萄酒，一直对此感到疑惑。但是，那些葡萄酒真的能够保存那么久吗？ 在我安顿下来后，我简单地参观了一下酒窖。虽然那位前女王的食量很大，但宫殿储备的酒量也同样充足。这些酒窖已经使用了两百多年，现在的储酒量还只有总量的一半稍少一些。哈，那些苍白精灵们肯定非常喜欢他们的葡萄酒……” “镜之酒，也就是其他民族更常称之为冰酒的这种饮品，它的制作原料可不仅仅是葡萄；它是多种食材精心调配而成的。 [silly |十一种秘制的浆果、草药和香料 |各种水果和草药 ] 这些作物是由德鲁伊们经过数代人的努力才培育出来的。在过去，我们面临着巨大的生产压力，但我们总是严格遵守每年的配额，直到无法再继续满足要求为止。正是通过这种方式，我们才赢得了普通布尔阿尔瓦人的尊重——因为我们愿意在必要时亲自动手部干活，不畏惧付出努力。那么这其中并没有什么神奇之处吗？” 赫希娅笑了：“那些霜冻领主的王子们过去总说肯定有什么神奇的秘密，但实际上，酿酒的过程并没有什么魔力，也没有什么神秘的成分；所有的制作方法和技术都是经过漫长岁月不断改进和完善而来的。 镜之酒是文化、灵性的象征，也是人们对荒野进行审慎保护的象征。如今，随着各种变化的发生，它很可能会赋予新的含义，但这些含义依然与原有的意义相似。 与她所信仰的宗教中其他逐渐消失的元素相比，她对这一变化似乎并没有那么愤懑。尽管我心中充满苦涩，但我想我们大家都会认同：Mirrorwine这种饮品绝对不应该从Savarra的土地上消失。即使它已经失去了原有的意义，但它的味道本身依然承载着人们对过去的回忆。" |那么，接下来是什么呢？ 是 关于对“古老荒野”的崇拜，你至今应该已经听了很多相关内容。在这种信仰体系中， 霜林地区的古老荒野树木某种程度上被视作神灵的象征——但又不完全是神灵；这种信仰也算不上是一种严格的宗教体系……但那么，它的具体信条和准则究竟是什么呢？ “我知道你没有恶意 [pc.name]不过，即便如此，要描述一种正在我们眼前消亡的宗教，确实有点困难。请给我一点时间，让我整理一下思路，然后再详细说明。” “哦，当然。即使她无法完全向你解释清楚——而且你也不期望自己能完全理解其中的内涵——但只要她尝试去解释，你还是会感激她的。 我想，你可以把这种信仰称为一种万物有灵论。也就是说，物体、地点以及生物都蕴含着某种力量，而这些力量有时会表现出智慧与个性。当那些‘布尔阿尔瓦’在霜林中游荡时，我们这些德鲁伊们主要致力于与森林中的这些力量达成一种合理的共存关系——这样我们就可以获取所需的资源，安全地穿梭于森林的小径之间，在松树的荫蔽下建造居所，同时也要为自然界留出足够的空间。 那些野树并非南方人所理解的那种神明——尽管它们力量强大，但远称不上无所不能，它们的影响范围仅限于霜木地带，而在你们所称的旧森林地区，这种影响则更为有限。 然而，在他们所处的领域里，他们拥有巨大的影响力。他们渴望成为布尔阿尔瓦人集体记忆的一部分，作为交换，他们希望自己能被人们尊崇、照料，甚至可以说被崇拜。的确，虽然许多德鲁伊从森林和峡湾中的精灵那里获取力量，但在这些具有灵性的存在中，野生树木无疑处于最重要的地位。它们会为那些忠于它们的人赐予魔法与力量。" 你明白的。 “我认为我们其实并没有什么真正的戒律，至少不像那些崇拜南方诸神的人那样。我们与那些野生树木建立的是一种更为亲密、更为个人化的关系——我们每天都会与它们互动，如果愿意的话，甚至可以直接与它们对话。对于它们所说的话，我们也并不会去进行什么复杂的解读或诠释。 真的 我的意思是，因为任何人都可以直接去询问那些古老的树木它们的意图——每一棵树都存在着某种联系，如果其中一棵树知道了什么，其他的树木也会知晓。当“神战”首次降临到我们的边境时，这座冬日之城几乎在战争开始的同时就得到了消息。你现在应该开始明白这会走向何方了。其实这是一种小规模的宗教形式，每个群体都根据当地野生树木的特性与需求，形成了自己独特的习俗；这些信仰的核心在于与自然世界建立和谐关系，而在组织结构上，这种宗教通常采用相当宽松的管理模式——人们被赋予很大的自由度，可以按照自己所服务群体的需求来行事，而无需遵循统一的规范或标准。 虽然你肯定知道其中蕴含着许多微妙的差别，但至少赫希娅给了你一个开始讨论的依据，这已经很不错了。 他露出了一丝懊悔的笑容：“亲身经历是一回事， [pc.name]还有另一部分内容，则是为了帮助那些可能无法立刻理解这些概念的人，将这些内容用语言表达出来。 ] ] ]
rows.raw: " [var0 |[rand |"I... to be honest, when I suggested the whole Xadaron Temple thing, I didn't imagine it'd pay off this well. Mie obviously had a soft spot for her granddad, having been raised on stories of him, but I'd have expected the rest of them to push back a bit harder. For everyone to become a whole lot more reasonable just like that... it's kind of crazy." Was it? As you understood it, the realization that the corrupted wyld trees might not all be dead but instead biding their time might have instilled a sense of urgency in even the most stubborn of the archdruid's colleagues. "It's more the younger ones about Mie's age that're still opposed to the final agreement — the elder druids are like our remaining wyld tree, tired of it all and want to see things done before their time is up. That's a sentiment I'm beginning to respect more and more these days. "Either way, you don't have to worry about it. I'm sure a couple of years spent rebuilding the temple village will mellow them out, hard work has a habit of doing that." Are they going to rebuild Xadaron Temple? From the report, the valkyries caved in the old one during their clean-up so the ground would be more stable and suited to building. "Mmm, there's no reason to, really. The great temples were built to house the wyld trees, and this one's gone; we druids may remain as magicians and artisans, amongst other things, but we're no longer to be purveyors of faith." Hethia sighs and slowly shakes her head, as if she herself can't quite believe it. "The ley-line's still there, so I suppose something may be built there in the future, just not a temple." The future is bright, isn't it? "I don't know if that was meant to be a pun for that sun goddess, but yes, things are looking up from when I was dealing with a bunch of loggers on the other side of the River Ridell." |So, you've been wondering... "Yes?" After all that you've been through together and the way events have shaken out, can you ask her a question? "That depends on what it is. Ask." Back in the Old Forest, when she was, uh, dealing with those loggers... what was that thing that they were getting too close to that she wouldn't tell you or them about? Hethia raises an eyebrow. "You're still thinking about that?" It's what sparked off this lovely relationship that led to this point, after all. If she hadn't been there... if you hadn't been there... would you be here today? Surely now that the druids are letting go of their past and finding a new, more secular role within boreal elf society, perhaps she could tell a friend what that was all about? "I...guess. After what you've done for us, it's not right to treat you like an outsider any longer." Hethia thinks a moment. "The loggers were getting pretty close to one of the burial barrows of one of the archdruids dating from before the Godswar. It was a bothersome situation — if I'd told them what it was, someone would almost certainly go and try to find it. If I told them where to keep away from, that would've given away the general location, and that can be enough to find one of the old burial mounds that've been robbed over the years." And so she saw no choice but to get them to stop altogether, which in turn meant taking their livelihoods away as far as the short term was concerned. But was it so bad, really? One supposes someone in her position couldn't have trusted loggers she met mere days ago. "It's always more complicated than it appears at first glance." No doubt. "But now you know. Happy?" Actually? Yes. Now you have a beginning and an end, or at least where your involvement in this tale is concerned. Thanks. "Don't mention it." |"I wish I could've been with you while you were exploring Xadaron Temple. The things that you saw..." Would likely have revulsed her even more than you did them. And with her druidic magics being completely ineffective against the dangers the infested temple held, she would've been a burden even if she didn't immediately wind up infected with her first breath of spores. Oh gods, the spores, you still remember them — thick and choking, getting into all your cracks and corners. It she wants your honest opinion, it's better that she keeps her mental image of the glory of the druids, rather than see quiet literally how far they fell." Hethia swallows hard. "I guess you're right. Hearing you tell it, I'm not sure how I would've reacted to the corrupted wyld tree. That kind of betrayal, even if she was corrupted... were the Wraiths so powerful that they could have twisted her mind to such a degree? Did she always have a seed of malice that just needed the opportunity to sprout?" The way the wyld tree spoke to you, you get the impression that she saw infesting all the druids with the fungal infection as merely sharing a good thing with them, whether they liked it or not. "That's just as bad in a different way. If the Wraiths could make us perceive evil as good by just tilting the lens a little..." Hethia pauses mid-sentence and shakes her head. "You know what? You're right — even if I were somehow made impervious to infection by that fungus, I wouldn't want to have followed you down into the temple. It would've still been a learning experience, but the cost wouldn't have been worth it." |So, how are her colleagues taking the whole agreement thing? Before, the impression you got was that the talks could've taken years if they'd seriously dragged out; for something this important, even shorter-lived, more impulsive peoples would've taken longer than this, held out for better terms. "Some people do think that we should've done just that, but our wyld tree's already cautioned against demanding a mile after taking an inch. With the archdruid herself having made the call for it herself, no one's going to gainsay the decision already made, so..." What the young complainers need is a year or two getting the old temple village back into shape. Something to spend all their energy on instead of chasing tails. "Some of them aren't too keen on setting off just yet — there's some understandable suspicion that this is a trap of some sort, that the valkyries didn't clear out all of the infectious fungus, that the moment they get too close they'll be infested with Wraith-taint and turned into monsters." Hethia sighs. "It's a little ironic that there's more enthusiasm for the resettlement from the common people of Njorhaalt — even without us adding to the headcount, the city's been getting quite crowded this last decade, or so Elthara tells me. That's one of the reasons why Daliza was sent out to Dracia." When are the first people heading out for the whole resettlement thing, anyway? "Soon enough. It's not just about putting out the call for people, but the palace is also gathering the necessary provisions to supply said settlers for about a year until some kind of self-sufficiency can be achieved. It doesn't have to be all at once, but still the necessary goods needed to embark isn't something to sniff at. The mood of the people has been pretty good ever since Alissa's ouster, so there's no shortage of volunteers, we just have to figure out how to squeeze blood from the proverbial rock of the empty treasury." Good luck with the whole thing. Another sigh. "You know... all this wouldn't have been possible without you, [pc.name]. So I'm going to say it again — thanks for everything you've done." |So, you've been meaning to ask ever since you encountered a wyld tree for yourself: the last uncorrupted wyld tree that still lives, the druids' current patron... Hethia squints at you, reading your expression, then thins her lips at the unspoken question. "She's dying, yes. You know that." You understand that this is blunt, but how long will it take? The one you met in the ruins of Xadaron Temple seemed hale and hearty enough — too hale and hearty, given the nature of her corruption. At the same time, you also figure that the timeline the boreal elves and the wyld trees operate on isn't the same as most other Savarran peoples, so what's soon to them might be considerably longer in absolute terms. "We... we don't know for sure. It could be a year. The tree herself says no more than a decade, she can feel it in her roots. We can only hope that there's enough time for us to be weaned off our old habits and adopt new ones. It's less a physical thing, [pc.name], and more a spiritual one. "I'm not going to deny it, delivering the truth of what'd happened at Xadaron Temple to our patron diminished her will to live considerably. She said... she said she'd always suspected something like that, but had no proof of it. Now she's even more convinced that the time of her and her siblings is now over." You're — Hethia holds out a hand. "We don't want or need your pity or trite apologies. What you did — what I recommended you do — was the right thing, and there's no need to second-guess ourselves, especially after the fact. Our patron herself said that dying knowing the truth is better than living and always wondering, always suspecting... we've made important strides forward towards the future of late, so let's focus on that when there aren't any more lessons to be learned from this bit of past. Just moping around is going to make the parting worse." |So, now that the talks are more or less concluded, what's Hethia going to do from here on out? Is she going to leave with the rest of the druidic delegation? Is she going to help with the rebuilding of Xadaron Temple? "To be frank, I'm not completely sure," Hethia replies, tapping her chin and looking thoughtful. "Elthara's suggested that I stay on at the palace as a liaison, but that decision isn't in my hands. If the archdruid or my elders say that I'm needed somewhere else, I go, no questions asked. "Truth be told, I like it here in the palace. Norathar's getting along great with the other wargs in the kennels, and the creature comforts are very appealing. I can see why the druids of old were very reluctant to give up their station in boer'alvar society of the past." So, she's going to be leaving? "I didn't say anything of the kind, and if it does happen it probably won't be any time soon. I'll be in the palace for the foreseeable future, helping to put together provisions for the resettlement effort and making sure that the terms of the reunification are adhered to — by both sides, of course." Well, you're glad for that. Since Hethia entered the palace about the same time as you did, you've gotten used to her being as much of a fixture as you are, if not more. You aren't the only person who'd miss her if she were to have to pull up her roots. "That's... well, thank you for the compliment. And please be careful out there, especially when you're dragging our dear var Ridell with you. It wouldn't be the same without you around." ] |[hethia.isHostile |[rand |Hethia glares over her shoulder at you. "What does it matter? Once these talks are over, we're going to be effectively disbanded. What would you gain from learning about a soon to be dead way of life? Why would you bother to do such a thing save to mock us?" Because even though the druidic faith of the pale elves may eventually come to be dissolved, the impact it's had on its adherents lingers — the Winter City is proof of that. Even after two and a half centuries after abandoning those ways and practices and the current generation of pale elves having grown up knowing nothing but the worship of Lumia, she can still tell that there's some measure of the Old Wyld in their culture and blood, repurposed as it may be. That sort of thing doesn't wash out in one generation, or two, or six, if ever. That's why it's important for you to understand it while there's still someone around who can explain it effectively to you. Now then, what was the worship of the Old Wyld all about? You've heard a whole lot about it to date, and that the ancient wyld trees of the Frostwood were kind of a stand-in for deities-but-not-quite-deities for this religion-but-not-quite-religion, but what exactly are its tenets and precepts, anyway? Even if she can't fully explain it to you — and you don't expect to perfectly comprehend it, either — you'd appreciate it if she made the attempt. Hethia coughs. Why, does she still not want to tell you? It can't be helped if she's still not convinced, but — "No, no, I'll tell you about us and our beliefs, to get you off my back if nothing else. "I suppose you could call it a form of animism. That there are powers in objects, places and living things, and sometimes these manifest with intelligence and personality. When the boer'alvar ranged throughout the Frostwood, the druidic circles mostly busied ourselves with negotiating a reasonable coexistence between us and the powers present in the Frostwood, such that we might take what we needed and traverse its glades and trails safely, that we could build under the pine canopy so long as we kept spaces within artifice for the natural world. "The wyld trees are not gods as someone from the south would understand the term — while powerful, they certainly do not approach omnipotence, and their reach only extends to the Frostwood and to a lesser extent, the lands you know as the Old Forest. Yet within their domain, they hold much sway, and were eager to serve as a collective memory of sorts for the boer'alvar in exchange for being enshrined, cared for, and some might say, worshipped. Certainly, while many druids drew power from the spirits of the forests and fjords, the wyld trees were first and foremost amongst these animistic entities, and granted magics and powers to those who were faithful to them." You see. "I don't think we actually had any true precepts, not in the way that those who worship the southern gods do. It was a closer, more personal relationship where we interacted with the wyld trees every day and could converse with them directly if we had the mind to. There weren't any clever interpretations of what they really meant, because anyone could simply go up and ask the wyld trees of their intentions — each and every one of them had a link of sorts, where if one of them knew something, the rest would, too. When the Godswar first came upon our borders, the winter city knew of it almost immediately after it began..." You're starting to see where this is headed. Small-scale religion of sorts, each with their own customs in accordance with the local wyld tree's quirks and desires; beliefs focused on mediation with the natural world, and by and large a fairly loose hierarchy in which individuals were given a lot of leeway to do as they wished with the sensibilities of the people they served taken into accord as opposed to universal standards. While you're sure there's a lot of nuance, Hethia's at least given you something to start with, and that's good. A disdainful snort. "We'll see about that; I still don't expect someone like you to understand. It's one thing to live it, [pc.name], and another to try and put it into words for someone who might not find it all immediately obvious." |You're given to understand that the pale elf druids were guardians of the forest of sorts, then. Certainly she mentioned during the audience with Ryn that the whole reason she went after Westbank was because their logging operations were encroaching upon one of the remaining wyld trees. "I suppose you think it stupid, then," Hethia says with a sniff. "I had to tell them to stay away, yet wouldn't tell them where they needed to stay away from." Well, it's not so much stupid as she was caught between conflicting demands of her beliefs and allegiances. While an unpleasant situation for anyone to find themselves in, it's not as if it's a situation that's unique to her and hers. "Ever so carefully diplomatic, I see." This is a diplomatic matter, of course you should be diplomatic. There's a begrudging silence, and at last Hethia shrugs. "I guess you could've called us that, yes. None of that whole dancing in the woods naked nonsense to 'reconnect with your roots' — that's just trash that [pc.ra elf |wyld elves like you |wyld elves ] spout when they go back into the woods to have an excuse to fuck around, and other peoples can't tell the difference between one stripe of elf and another. As far as our so-called guardianship of the forest went about, it was about interacting with the numerous minor spirits that make up the forests and fjords; within the domain of the Frostwood, the wyld trees might have been the greatest and most prominent amongst them, but all lands are possessed of a bewildering array of minor spirits and entities whom we as the boer'alvar needed to entreat with in our daily lives. The whole 'guardian of the forest' thing is true inasmuch as if the land is damaged, its spirits are, too; hence, we were charged with preventing that from happening." See, things are so much clearer and unpleasantness so easily avoided if she would just explain things. "Should they become angered, we were summoned to address the source of that anger and placate them, resolve the root of the problem at hand; as we lived in the Frostwood at the time, what perturbed them would also perturb us. It was a symbiotic relationship of sorts... as druids, we were able to interact better with the world than the spirits of the forests and fjords were, especially upon the fringes of or outside their domains, and in turn we drew power from them. Before the arrival of the southern goddess Lumia, these spirits were always on the fringes of our lives, and once sin, incompetence and cruelty reared their heads amongst the boer'alvar they would be angered and lead them to punish or torment said people until the spirits were placated." It sounds like they were more guardians of the people than guardians of the forest. Hethia purses her lips. "More mediators than anything else. But then, I wouldn't expect even a boer'alvar of the Winter City to understand, let alone someone like you, so you can't be blamed for your ignorance — it requires one to draw upon a frame of reference that you simply don't have." |What exactly are the wyld trees, anyway? Are they the gods that the druids worship? Hethia scowls. "Of course you'd make that mistake. No, the wyld trees aren't gods in the way that you would understand them, like these Seven that all of the world now pays reverence to. They are powerful, yes, they are spiritual in nature, but I would hesitate to call them gods. They are just very, very old trees who have been tended to by generations of druids, and remember things very well. When you get to that kind of stage and accumulate that kind of power within yourself, it's conceivable that one might be mistaken for a deity, but no... they are powerful spirits that are aware of their own limitations and have no such delusions of grandeur. Consider them merely very ancient grandparents that you might have, capable and wise, but still approachable and relatable should you make the effort." The pale elves built temples to them, though. They worshipped them, and the druids served much the same purpose as the Lumian priests do now in pale elf society. While you can accept that they might be different in essence and nature, practically as they are — correction, were — to the pale elves they may as well have been gods. Hethia sniffs. "I suppose I can't say that you're wrong, but it's more like respecting and acknowledging your grandmother's power and prowess than any kind of divine reverence. The acknowledgement that they're older, wiser and more worldly than you are, if nothing else. The difference is important." And some people engage in ancestor worship. But yes, you think you see the point. "It's undeniable that your gods exist, [pc.name]. I can't just set aside the evidence of my own eyes, not when they're walking around and granting small miracles to their worshippers every day. But there are other spiritual powers in Savarra that aren't them and aren't gods in the same way that they are, and some of those have accumulated considerable power over time. The wyld trees fall into that category. And now those who did not pass in the Godswar have accepted their passing at the hands of time, for all good that their immortality has done them." ... "If you accumulate enough power, you might become something like them. If anyone did, to be honest. It's getting to that point that's the tricky part." |"We used to produce much of the wine that the boer'alvar drank. It was, and still is a point of pride for us — one of the first things I did was to go down into the palace's wine cellars and see how well-stocked they were after more than two centuries. I must say, I'm rather pleased." Is that right? You've seen some of the vintages served here in the palace of ice, and you always wondered. But could the wine have lasted that long? Hethia sneers. "While the var Ridell line predictably descended into worthless debauchery and their appetites were massive, so were the reserves the palace had in store. More than two hundred years of use, and they were only a little under half full." Huh. the pale elves must have really loved their wine... "Mirrorwine, or ice wine as it's more commonly known to other peoples, is made from more than just grapes; it's a careful blend of [silly |eleven secret berries, herbs and spices |various fruits and herbs ] that've been cultivated for many generations by the druids. In times past, there was considerable pressure for us to produce as much as possible, but we always stuck to the yearly quotas before telling the crown no more. It was how we earned respect in the eyes of the common boer'alvar, to show that we weren't afraid of getting our hands dirty when need be." And there's no magic in the wine or the vinting process? The sneer widens. "No, we don't cheat. The frostmander princes used to say it must have been, but no, there's nothing magical about the vinting process, or mystical secret ingredients involved in its making; both hows and whos alike have just been refined and perfected over a long, long time. Mirrorwine is a symbol of culture, of spirituality, of careful stewardship of the Wyld, and now that things are changing, it will likely take on new, but similar meanings." She sounds a lot less bitter about this than the other aspects of her religion fading away... "Bitter as I may be, I think we can all agree that Mirrorwine is something that should not vanish from the face of Savarra. Even if it loses its meaning, its taste alone carries with it the memories of its past; as much as I think the Winter City doesn't deserve to have the secrets of its making, we are all given boons we don't deserve every day. Deserve has nothing to do with it, as the saying goes." |"What's the point?" Come again? "I mean it. Why are you even bothering to ask this question? We're dying. We'll soon be dead. All these negotiations with the Winter City are merely making arrangements to commit at least a somewhat dignified suicide instead of wasting away over the next two or three decades — tying up all the loose ends so that at least we schismatics aren't left to rot when the dust blows over. It's dressed up in pretty words and sweet gestures, but I know Elthara's hiding a stupid smirk every time she sits down on the opposite end of the table. She and her ilk have won, and she knows it." Look, maybe she's sounding a little bitter, but — "Bitter? Of course I'm bitter. Why shouldn't I be bitter? The realization that all of my life, all of our lives working away to stave off this end, or something like it, has been meaningless and I might as well have spent my time doing something else? You resent me for taking those loggers hostage — well, that has also been made meaningless by this. Nothing's changed, the end for the Old Wyld and its druidic circles still looms, and the only choice left to us is how we want to die, rather than the choice to die at all. That sense of meaningless nothingness — wouldn't you be bitter at the sense of cosmic injustice, too?" See, if she'd let you get in a word edgewise, the point is that it doesn't have to be a waste. It must be something, to hear stories of such a time while sitting in its ruins. Does she ever wish she could have experienced that golden age for herself? Hethia shakes her head. "Tempting, but no. It would have its merits, but that era of our history was also too peaceful for the likes of someone like me. The stories are nice, but I'm one more for conflict, and this age of the boer'alvar need those like me." The stories... "Yes, the stories. Anyone can easily see for themselves that they're not cooked up from simple nostalgia — the Frostwood is rife with elven ruins all the way down to the river by the south." That's right, you've had to pass the Wayfort and the adjoining old stone bridge on your way up to the Winter City. It was where you met Ryn, after all. "That Wayfort used to garrison anywhere from between thirty to fifty outriders and their mounts; the bridge and river marked the border between lands claimed by the boer'alvar and the lupine tribes, the latter of which later was consumed by the Belharan Empire. It was the first of the outposts to fall when the troubles began..." Then for as much to remain as it has, the worksmanship must have been something in its heyday. "By your standards, our buildings last well. By our standards, they are annoying things that constantly demand maintenance every decade or so," Hethia replies with a thin smile. "But since the end of the Godswar and the resultant schism in our people, there was no need to maintain the Wayfort, nor any of the outrider outposts in the Frostwood." The outriders no longer existed? "Oh, a good number survived the fighting, that's for sure, and they still continued to patrol the Frostwood. But where they once did so to keep the trails and paths safe from the forest's more unfriendly denizens and other darker creatures from beyond, now they did it to keep the Winter City safe from us. Atheldred was not unreasonably concerned that we wouldn't be content in our exile, self-imposed as it was... and to be fair, the early years saw several calls for and a handful of isolated incidents of surreptitious strikes against the people who had rejected us, who had embraced this new, foreign goddess." ... Even after all this, no one really wanted to pit sister against sister." Hethia sighs. "For a couple of centuries, the outsiders made cursory patrols of the Frostwood's fringes; we'd ignore them, and they'd ignore us. And then, a couple decades ago, they stopped coming altogether." If you remember right, that should have been around when Alissa took the throne... which makes perfect sense. She'd have seen no need to continue the patrols, seeing them as a waste of resources that could've been frittered away in decadence. "And when the outriders departed then it was just us, in the ruins of what used to be our glory." Hethia finishes with a sigh. "Born too early to see the schism mended, too late to have enjoyed any of the glories while they lasted — and just in time to fight tooth and nail for our future. It's getting to that point that's the tricky part." |How did the druids make a living in the Frostwood? You're guessing that they didn't farm in the commonly accepted sense, but did they just use their powers to make fruit fall from the bough, or... "By the Wyld, not that kind of nonsense, none of it at all! That's just trash that [pc.ra elf |wyld elves who're less scrupulous than you |wyld elves ] spout when they go back into the woods to 'reconnect with their roots', as it were. "I know you don't mean malice, [pc.name], but even so it can be a little hard to speak of a religion that's dying before your eyes. Give me a moment to gather myself, please, and then I'll elaborate." Oh, of course.
